anchors.fact: One of the stories people told about his memory: a guest sailed to England, stayed ten years, and walked back into the bar. Willard greeted him by name, recalled his old room number and remarked "how quickly ten years roll away" (Oxford, WILLARD, ORSAMUS pdf 2193, which frames it as one of the common stories of his memory).
anchors.meaning: Someone had kept him in mind the whole time he was gone. That's the feeling of being expected.
anchors.speaksTo: gives: the feeling of being expected

anchors.fact: At the City Hotel the bar was also the front desk: guests checked in at the bar (Oxford pdf 2192; *Imbibe!* pdf 20). Among the stories told of him: he almost never left the hotel (Oxford pdf 2193, "stories of his eccentricities").
anchors.meaning: He was always the first thing a guest met, and always already there.
anchors.speaksTo: the care lives in the getting ready; staying put, having it ready

anchors.fact: His own house back in Massachusetts had numbers on every room door (Oxford pdf 2193–94, "number plates on every room door"; *Imbibe!* pdf 22, "room numbers on every door").
anchors.meaning: I like to think he was still getting rooms ready for guests (our reading, signposted: the page gives no reason). The same kind of number he'd remembered for a guest.
anchors.speaksTo: the empty table; a place ready for people who might not come

anchors.fact: Willard left no book of recipes and no account of his life, and even the basic facts took a historian "a great deal of digging" (*Imbibe!* pdf 22).
anchors.meaning: He kept everyone in mind, and almost nobody wrote him down. That's attention running one way (our reading).
anchors.speaksTo: fear: attention that only runs one way; few think to know them back

anchors.fact: A British army captain who drank at the City Hotel printed a short list of drink recipes in his travel book, *Transatlantic Sketches* (1833). The Apple-toddy is the one he credits to Willard by name, "the bar-keeper of the City Hotel, who never forgets the face of a customer" (J. E. Alexander, 1833, vol. 2, p. 300, read on the page).
anchors.meaning: A guest wrote him down, and that's how his toddy reached us (never "the only reason"). The care came back (our reading, signposted; the captain's motive isn't on record).
anchors.speaksTo: the care came back; gives, and rarely asks back

anchors.fact: Willard's Apple-toddy, in his reported words: the fairest apples rolled in brown paper wetted with water, buried in live embers until thoroughly roasted and quite soft; then a fourth part each of apples, brandy and water, a lump of ice, "rich" with a fourth part of sugar (Alexander 1833, vol. 2, p. 300).
anchors.meaning: Everything is done before anyone arrives. When a guest walks in, there's only the stir and the ice.
anchors.speaksTo: the love happens before anyone arrives

anchors.fact: The captain's page says only "brandy". "Plain grape brandy" is Wondrich's reading of Willard's preference (*Imbibe!* pdf 139). "VSOP cognac" is Wondrich's modern advice, not Willard's.
anchors.meaning: The spirit Willard would have poured, as far as the record reaches.

anchors.fact: Loved in America "from the beginning of the Republic… until the turn of the last century", and early on "something of a signifier of Americanness" (*Imbibe!* pdf 138). The Apple Toddy was, with the Cock-Tail and the Mint Julep, one of the canonic drinks that made the American bar famous abroad (Oxford, COCK-TAIL pdf 494). It was enjoyed in the eastern US for over two hundred years (Oxford, TODDY pdf 2035). After Repeal, "Apple Toddy was seen no more" (*Imbibe!* pdf 139).
anchors.meaning: A renowned classic that people stopped making. Worth bringing back for someone.
anchors.speaksTo: let the drink sound worth having

anchors.fact: Wondrich thinks Willard "probably made do" with four or five kinds of glass: small and large tumblers, small and large wineglasses, perhaps cordial glasses, and something for hot drinks (*Imbibe!* pdf 55).
anchors.meaning: A small wineglass is a kind of glass his bar would probably have had. That's Wondrich's estimate, so no "his glass".

anchors.fact: "The apples go in first, then you call the one you're hoping will come": the roasting as the invitation.
anchors.meaning: The guest's ask, never Willard's. The record has him being lured back, never asking.
anchors.speaksTo: position: ask; ends on what they gain

cocktail.closingLine: Roast the apples. While they cool, call the one you'd most like to see.
cocktail.glassware: a small wineglass (about 250 ml), one plain lump of ice
method: An hour or more before anyone comes, peel and core the apples, half an apple for each drink. Wet a sheet of brown paper (a brown paper bag soaked under the tap works), wrap each apple in it, and roast at 180°C (350°F) for 30 to 45 minutes, until the apples are completely soft. Willard buried his in the embers of a fire. Let them cool.
Put half a roasted apple and the sugar in the glass, and mash them together with a spoon.
Add the brandy and the cold water, and stir until the sugar has gone and the apple is loose in the drink. Do this before anyone arrives, in the glass or in a jug for several. It will wait.
When they come, give it a stir, add one lump of ice, stir a few more turns, and serve with the spoon in the glass.
cocktail.name: Hoping You'd Come

recipe.item: roasted apple (roughly half a medium apple, peeled and cored)
recipe.note: wrapped in wet brown paper and roasted until soft, as Willard's recipe has it. Then left to cool.

recipe.item: brandy (grape brandy: a VSOP cognac, or any aged grape brandy of about 40%)
recipe.note: the captain's page says only "brandy"; Wondrich reads it as the grape brandy he preferred
Willard used as much sugar as brandy; I cut it to a teaspoon and a half, or it would be more than four times too sweet

cocktail.tagline: You make room for people before you ask them to come.

reading.epigraph: A captain wrote this toddy down from a barman who, people said, never forgot a face.
whoYouAre: Someone's coming over. Long before they get there, you've been at it: the chair moved nearer the heater for the one who always feels the cold, the music down to where people can talk, the light just so. By the time they walk in, it looks as if it all happened by itself. That's the idea. Nobody should feel they put you to any trouble. They should just feel expected.

What you'd never tell them is: I was hoping you'd come. All that getting ready is how you hope without asking. A room made ready can't be turned down, and a plain question can. The thought you don't let yourself stay with is the ready room with nobody in it. Here's what people take home from your evenings, even when they couldn't say why: the feeling that someone had them in mind before they arrived.
yours: In New York, back when hotel guests checked in at the bar, the City Hotel's desk clerk and its bartender were the same man, Orsamus Willard. People told a story about him. A guest sailed to England, stayed ten years, and walked back into the bar. Willard greeted him by name, and remembered his old room number.

They said he almost never left the hotel, and that he'd do anything he could to make a guest comfortable. He left no book and no account of his own life, and even the plain facts of it are hard to find. When he went home to Massachusetts, his house had a number on every room door. I like to think he was still getting rooms ready, for guests who might or might not come.
That's where I see you in him. Not the famous memory. The rooms made ready anyway.

One of his guests did write his toddy down. A British army captain who drank at his bar printed a few recipes in his travel book, and credited one of them to Willard by name: the Apple Toddy, one of the renowned drinks that made the American bar famous abroad. After Prohibition, it all but disappeared. The cocktail I've made for you is made after Willard's: the best apples rolled in wet paper and roasted until soft, then equal measures of apple, brandy and water, as he had them, and one lump of ice. His called for as much sugar as brandy, far too sweet by today's taste, so I kept it to a teaspoon and a half. For the brandy, I took the grape brandy the historian David Wondrich believes Willard preferred. Nearly all of it happens before anyone arrives: the apples roast, cool and wait. I kept it that way as a nod to you, because that's where your care always starts.

So next time you're getting a room ready, add the one thing you always leave out. Ask. Not "come by sometime": the plain sentence, to the person you're hoping will come. Getting ready is how you hope. Asking is how they find out they were hoped for. And I wish you a full house.
